c.tagline: France's rugged Mediterranean port — bouillabaisse, calanques, and salty soul.

taxi.fareNote: City taxis are metered, but the run to/from Marseille Provence Airport is a fixed fare of about €50 by day and €58 at night. Book by app or find a stand; street-hailing is uncommon.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number reaching police, ambulance, and fire; within France, 17 is police, 15 is the SAMU medical service, and 18 is fire.

avoid.reason: Drug-related violence in the northern districts (Quartiers Nord) — avoid; pickpocketing around the Vieux-Port, Noailles and Gare Saint-Charles

hood_desc: Marseille's beating heart, where fishermen still sell the morning catch on the quay and cafes fill for sunset aperitifs; the most central, walkable base with easy access to MuCEM, Le Panier, and the boats out to the Calanques.

The city's oldest quarter, a maze of steep, narrow lanes draped in laundry and street art, dotted with artisan boutiques, galleries, and the 17th-century Vieille Charite; atmospheric and photogenic, best for those who want old-Marseille character.

A hip, bohemian hilltop district about 15 minutes' walk from the port, covered in murals and lined with independent shops, record stores, artisan coffee, and lively bars around Place Jean Jaures; a magnet for creatives and night owls.

A relaxed seaside stretch along the Corniche Kennedy, with the Vallon des Auffes fishing cove, cliffside villas, and small beaches; quieter and residential, ideal for travellers who want sea views and a calmer pace.
lodging: Radisson Blu Hotel, Marseille Vieux Port

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the city.

transit.hours: The metro runs roughly 5:00am to 12:30am (until ~1:00am Fri-Sat); RTM buses run into the evening, with night lines N1 and N2 leaving the Vieux-Port from about 1:30am to 4:30am.
transit.note: The historic Ferry Boat has shuttled passengers across the Vieux-Port between the two quays since 1880; RTM also runs seasonal Navettes Maritimes sea shuttles to Pointe Rouge, l'Estaque, and the Frioul islands.
transit.pay: The network is run by RTM. Buy single tickets (€1.80), day passes, or a reloadable transpass card at metro machines and tabacs; contactless bank cards and the RTM app also work. One ticket covers metro, tram, and bus with free transfers within 60 minutes.

ferry: Gare Maritime (Marseille Ferry Terminal, to Corsica, Sardinia, Algeria, Tunisia)

transit.m: Navette airport shuttle bus to Gare Saint-Charles (25-30 min, every 15-20 min)
LeBus+13 shuttle to Vitrolles-Aeroport station, then train to Saint-Charles (~35 min)

tip.r: Service is included by law (service compris), so tipping is not expected; rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good service is a kind gesture.

food.name: Bouillabaisse
food.desc: The city's totem fish stew: rockfish broth served first with rouille and croutons, then the poached fish carved at the table.

places.name: Chez Fonfon
places.note: Family-run since 1952 in the tiny fishing cove; the benchmark two-service bouillabaisse.

places.name: Le Miramar
places.note: Old Port institution and signatory of the bouillabaisse charter; fish filleted tableside.

places.name: L'Esplai du Grand Bar des Goudes
places.note: End-of-the-road fishing hamlet spot locals drive out to; book days ahead.

food.name: Panisse
food.desc: Chickpea-flour batter set firm, cut into sticks and fried golden - Marseille's original street snack, best with salt and lemon.

places.name: Les Panisses
places.note: Small kitchen built around the snack; panisses fried to order all day.

places.name: Marche des Capucins
places.note: Daily market stalls sell hot panisses and chichis alongside North African spices.

places.name: Chez Magali
places.note: Seafront kiosk in the neighbourhood that claims the panisse; cash-friendly and quick.

food.name: Navette de Marseille
food.desc: Hard little boat-shaped biscuit scented with orange blossom, baked in the city since the 18th century and eaten with coffee.

places.name: Four des Navettes
places.note: Marseille's oldest bakery, open since 1781, still guarding the original recipe.

places.name: Les Navettes des Accoules
places.note: Tiny old-town bakery turning out navettes plus orange-blossom barquettes.

places.name: Marche des Capucins
places.note: Bags of navettes from several stalls if you want to compare recipes.

food.name: Pizza moitie-moitie
food.desc: Marseille's own wood-fired pizza, half anchovy-emmental and half tomato-cheese, folded and eaten standing at the counter.

places.name: Chez Etienne
places.note: Legendary no-menu, no-card pizzeria in the old town; expect to queue.

places.name: Chez Sauveur
places.note: Wood-fired since 1943 on rue d'Aubagne; the moitie-moitie template.

places.name: Chez Jeannot
places.note: Terrace over the fishing cove; pizza and a pastis at sunset.

food.name: Aioli garni
food.desc: Friday ritual: poached cod, snails and boiled vegetables around a mortar of raw-garlic mayonnaise thick enough to stand a spoon in.

places.name: Chez Madie Les Galinettes
places.note: Old Port terrace doing full Provencal classics including the Friday aioli.

places.name: L'Esplai du Grand Bar des Goudes
places.note: Seaside dining room where the aioli is a weekly fixture with the regulars.

places.name: Toinou Coquillages
places.note: Shellfish house handy for the raw bar and Provencal sides year-round.

food.name: Pieds et paquets
food.desc: Slow-braised lamb trotters and stuffed tripe parcels in white wine and tomato - the city's hardcore Sunday dish.

places.name: Chez Madie Les Galinettes
places.note: One of the few central kitchens still cooking it the long, traditional way.

places.name: Chez Fonfon
places.note: Classic Marseillais carte alongside the bouillabaisse; book ahead.

food.name: Pastis
food.desc: Anise spirit poured over ice and cut five-to-one with water until it clouds; the local aperitif clock starts around six.

places.name: La Maison du Pastis
places.note: Shop and tasting bar stocking dozens of small-producer pastis beyond the big brands.

places.name: Le Bar de la Marine
places.note: Old Port bar of Pagnol legend; pastis at the zinc with a harbour view.

places.name: La Caravelle
places.note: First-floor balcony bar above the quay, all wood panelling and sunset light.

food.name: Provence rose and vin de Cassis
food.desc: Pale Provencal rose and the crisp white of nearby Cassis, both drunk cold and young with anything from the sea.

places.name: La Part des Anges
places.note: Wine shop and bar with a deep Provencal list and small plates till late.

places.name: Les Buvards
places.note: Natural-wine bar near the harbour; helpful staff, blackboard by the glass.

landmarks: Notre-Dame de la Garde
This hilltop basilica crowned with a golden Virgin Mary statue offers the most breathtaking panoramic views over Marseille and the Mediterranean.
Vieux-Port (Old Port)
The bustling historic harbor at the heart of the city, lined with fishing boats, cafés, and the daily fish market, is the soul of Marseille.
MuCEM (Musée des Civilisations de l'Europe et de la Méditerranée)
A striking modern museum wrapped in a lace-like concrete latticework, connected to the old fort by a dramatic footbridge over the sea.
Le Panier
Marseille's oldest neighborhood, a maze of narrow pastel-colored streets covered in vibrant street art and mosaic tiles, perfect for wandering and photos.
Château d'If
The 16th-century island fortress made famous by 'The Count of Monte Cristo' sits just offshore, reachable by a scenic boat ride.
Cathédrale de la Major
An enormous Byzantine-Romanesque cathedral striped in green and white stone, dramatically positioned overlooking the harbor and sea.
Fort Saint-Jean
A medieval fortress guarding the entrance to the Old Port, now linked by footbridges to MuCEM and offering sweeping coastal views.
Palais Longchamp
A grand 19th-century monumental palace with cascading fountains, flanking colonnades, and gardens, housing the city's fine arts and natural history museums.
Calanques National Park
Dramatic limestone cliffs plunging into turquoise coves just outside the city form one of the most spectacular coastal landscapes in France.
Vallon des Auffes
A tiny, picture-perfect fishing cove with colorful wooden boats tucked beneath a stone bridge, one of the most photographed spots in Marseille.

train.note: Gare de Marseille Saint-Charles is a few hundred metres north of the centre at the top of a monumental staircase, with a metro connection if you have luggage. TGVs reach Paris in about 3 hours via Lyon, and Nice is roughly 2h30m along the coast. One direct high-speed train a day runs to Barcelona in about 4h35m; it is a Renfe service, so book on renfe.com where the cheapest fares appear, and there are several direct TGVs a day north to Brussels. Eurostar's direct London-Marseille summer train has not operated since 2019, so change at Paris or Lille. Local Zou! and TER fares are separate from TGV tickets.

bus.note: International and long-distance coaches use the Gare Routiere Saint-Charles, built into the side of the railway station, so transfers are simple. Barcelona is about 7 hours, Milan around 8 and Turin 6. Tickets are bought online in advance; the counters here mostly serve regional Zou! coaches (https://zou.maregionsud.fr/) to Aix, Cassis, Arles and the Camargue, which can be paid for on board. Carry a passport for services to Spain and Italy, and allow extra time in summer when the terminal is busy.

Ajaccio & Porto-Vecchio, Corsica (France) - from the Joliette terminal
Algiers, Bejaia & Skikda (Algeria) - from the Gare Maritime
Tanger Med (Morocco) - from the Joliette terminal

ferry.note: All ferries leave from the Gare Maritime de la Joliette, about 1.5 km north of the Vieux-Port and reachable by metro line 2 to Joliette. Corsican sailings are mostly overnight, take 9-12 hours and run daily to Ajaccio and Bastia, less often to Ile-Rousse, Propriano and Porto-Vecchio. North African crossings to Algiers, Bejaia, Skikda and Tunis take around 20 hours and run one or two times a week, with Algerie Ferries and CTN also serving these routes; they fill up months ahead in the summer emigration season and require visas and long check-in times. Cars and cabins must be booked well in advance for all overnight routes, and there is a separate local shuttle from the Vieux-Port to the Frioul islands and the Chateau d'If.

half.name: Cassis
half.blurb: A Provençal fishing port about thirty minutes east, the gateway to the calanques' turquoise inlets and cliffside coastal trails.

half.name: Aix-en-Provence
half.blurb: A university town about thirty minutes north known for tree-lined boulevards, fountains, and Paul Cézanne's former studio.

half.name: Avignon
half.blurb: A walled papal city about ninety minutes northwest, home to the Palais des Papes and the broken medieval Pont d'Avignon.
